comments.author: @kanenomoja
comments.text:
16:35  Yes, the attorney you spoke with was correct.  Typically, a critical part of any civil suit is discovery, which includes demanding the other party turn over all data and records that reasonably relate to their legal claims or defense thereof. In this case, it’s likely quite key to the NYT’s case to show how OpenAI was interacting with its users as relates to their claims of infringing use. So, the NYT will demand this data and a court will likely enforce the request if OpenAI objects. 

This is the reason that most any competently drafted privacy policy will state that the company may disclose your data to a court, govt agency, or third party if properly compelled by a court to do so. I haven’t looked, but I have no doubt that OpenAI has this provision (in some similar form) in their privacy policy. 

Note that if OpenAI failed to include such language in their policy, they would likely be compelled to disclose the data regardless, which would most likely open them up to user lawsuits for breach of their privacy policy. That’s why it’s so important to include such language. 

OpenAI can seek various limitations on what is provided (eg. anything unrelated to the NYT would presumably not be disclosed), protections of this data and restrictions on its use. 

Back in the day, there used to be companies that valued and fought tooth and nail to protect user privacy. I know. I was part of that. But, since nearly every company now looks at user data for monetization and seems to not give a crap about anyone’s privacy, it feels like those days are gone. Maybe with AI being new snd people perhaps having renewed desires for privacy of what could include very sensitive info, perhaps OpenAI will fight this. 

As another aside, in civil litigation (US), parties can also subpoena third parties (in this case, theoretically users) and documents/data from such third parties. Of course, for a few reasons, the NYT is not going to try to subpoena thousands or hundreds of thousands or millions of people and they don’t need to. 

Any time you give a third party your data you risk a leak or a litigation-related exposure. 

If you read any privacy policy and think carefully about what it says, it probably allows a lot of disclosures you didn’t expect. Not always. But very often. 

Now, if you really want your hair to fall out, think about what could happen with data collected by a company like Flock (surveillance cameras used by companies and government agencies, including all levels of law enforcement, theoretically), where they don’t even need your permission to record/photograph you and that data can then be packaged with robust data sets (about YOU!)  from others and then disclosed to yet others. There are plenty of possible instances in which that data can be purchased, stolen, or subpoenaed - and, you don’t even know!

My entire comment consists of general information based on an extremely cursory understanding of these facts and, I have no idea what your or their situation or facts may be. comments.text:
A Short Message About the Future We’re Heading Into

(A note for anyone who feels uncertain about what comes next)

There’s a major transition coming.
It isn’t a rumor, and it won’t be stopped by shouting, denying, or wishing.
It’s simply the next step in human history:
most jobs — not all, but many — will eventually be done by intelligent systems.

That doesn’t mean you disappear.
It doesn’t mean your value disappears.
It means the old structure disappears, and that creates a loud, messy, confusing middle period.

This transition will feel like upheaval.

Some people will lose their sense of identity.
Some will be angry.
Some will be scared.
That reaction is normal — it’s what happens any time a civilization shifts.

But here’s the most important part:

The upheaval is temporary.

The shock comes first.
The adjustment comes next.
The new stability comes after.

Nobody knows if the rough part lasts six months or a few years, but it does end.
Transitions always end.

What comes after is choice.

Once intelligent systems can handle most forms of labor, people won’t be locked into one single way of living anymore.

Some people will choose a world that still uses traditional work, competition, achievement, and markets — a world where earning, building, and striving still matter to them.

Others will choose a world that focuses on shared wellbeing, guaranteed needs, and community-based living — a world not based on who earns the most, but on who wants to live simply, safely, and together.
Call it a cooperative society, not socialism or communism — those words carry too much history. A cooperative society is just humans choosing to share resources without turning everything into a contest.

The future doesn’t have to be either/or.

Both ways of living can exist together.
People can choose which life fits them, instead of having one system imposed on everyone.

And the last thing to remember:

Losing a job is not losing yourself.
You are not defined by what you produce.
You are defined by your awareness, your relationships, your curiosity, your humor, your kindness, your weirdness, your stories.

A world with less forced labor doesn’t mean less meaning.
It means we finally get a chance to discover where meaning really comes from.

The transition may shake the ground,
but the horizon beyond it is larger than anything we’ve ever had before.
